Projective Differential Moment Invariants from the Viewpoint of Classical Invariant Theory

Leonid Bedratyuk Address: Khmelnytskyi National University, Insituts’ka st., 11, Khmelnytskyi, 29016, Ukraine Email address: leonidbedratyuk@khmnu.edu.ua
Abstract.

Polynomial first-order projective differential moment invariants are investigated. The main result establishes an exact correspondence between such moment invariants and symmetric polynomial multipoint relative projective differential invariants of weight −1-1. This correspondence provides an algebraic description of each homogeneous component, with respect to moment degree, of the space of polynomial projective differential moment invariants and makes it possible to use previously obtained results on relative projective invariants for their systematic construction. It is also proved separately that the passage from the formal algebra of moments to their integral definitions does not produce additional algebraic relations among the constructed invariants. For low moment degrees, the absence of nontrivial invariants of degrees 11 and 22 is established, and a complete description of the invariants of degree 33 is obtained. The ten cubic differential moments are naturally identified with the coefficients of a ternary cubic, thereby establishing a connection between the theory developed here and classical invariant theory. In particular, the Aronhold invariants SS and TT generate projective differential moment invariants of degrees 44 and 66. It is also shown that one of the known moment invariants of Wang et al. is proportional to the invariant SS. It is proved that the algebra of polynomial moment invariants is not finitely generated. It is also established that the field of rational moment invariants coincides with the field of fractions of the algebra of polynomial moment invariants. For the explicit constructions, compact multipoint representations are provided that define the corresponding moment polynomials without the need to write out their full expansions in the text. These representations provide a basis for the algorithmic construction and software computation of the invariants.

Keywords: projective moment invariants; differential moments; Lie algebra 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3}; relative invariants; polarization; ternary cubic; Aronhold invariants; symbolic method.

1. Introduction

Moment invariants are a classical tool for constructing global image characteristics that are insensitive to a prescribed class of geometric transformations. Since the work of Hu [1], an extensive theory of moment invariants has been developed for groups of rotations, scalings, similarity transformations, and affine transformations in general. Such invariants have found applications in pattern recognition, image registration, and object identification. A systematic account of the theory of moment invariants and their applications is given in [2].

Projective transformations present a more difficult case. Unlike the affine action, the Jacobian of a projective transformation depends on the coordinates of the point, and therefore a finite system of ordinary geometric moments is not closed under this action. This prevents the direct extension of classical affine constructions to the projective group. Several approaches have been proposed to overcome this obstacle. Suk and Flusser [3] considered representations of projective moment invariants by infinite series involving moments with positive and negative indices. Another approach uses additional geometric information. In particular, Wang, Zhang, and Yao [4] introduced co-moments constructed using two reference points. In this case, finite formulas are obtained at the cost of having to identify the corresponding points in the images.

An important line of research involves incorporating derivatives of the image function into moment kernels. Wang and coauthors [5] proposed a system of DD-moments that incorporates coordinates, intensity, and first derivatives, and used it to construct families of projective moment expressions. Li, Mo, Xu, and Li [6] refined this construction, studied relative projective differential invariants, and used them as weight functions to construct finite weighted moment invariants. Their proposed constructions involve higher-order derivatives of the intensity function, whose numerical estimation is substantially more sensitive to noise and discretization errors. Therefore, in this paper we restrict attention to first-order derivatives, seeking to preserve projective invariance with less numerical instability. Higher-order absolute projective image invariants are also considered in the work of Olver [7].

Previous studies have shown that using derivatives makes it possible to construct finite projective moment characteristics of images. However, the known constructions are largely restricted to individual invariant formulas or individual families of invariants, leaving aside the problem of systematically describing the entire algebra of polynomial projective differential moment invariants. This raises a structural problem: to provide a general algebraic description of all polynomial projective differential moment invariants and to construct a systematic mechanism for obtaining them that is not reduced to searching for individual invariant formulas. A further question concerns rational moment invariants: do they form the field of fractions of the algebra of polynomial invariants, that is, can every rational invariant be expressed as a ratio of two polynomial invariants?

By its nature, this question belongs to invariant theory. A similar viewpoint has already proved productive for ordinary geometric moments. In the work [8], algebras of two-dimensional geometric moment invariants were related to algebras of joint invariants of binary forms. This approach replaces the search for individual unwieldy expressions with the study of a common algebraic structure.

For the projective group, implementing an analogous program proved substantially more difficult. It was first necessary to develop a theory of multipoint projective differential invariants and to identify relative invariants whose transformation law compensates for the Jacobian of the projective change of variables. This problem was addressed successively in three previous papers by the author. In [9], the field of multipoint first-order projective differential invariants for nn points in the plane was described, explicit generators of the field of absolute invariants were constructed, and relative invariants associated with the Jacobian of the projective action were studied. In the work [10], the same problem was considered using the moving frame method. This provided a geometric way of obtaining fundamental multipoint projective differential invariants and made it possible to trace directly the emergence of the relative multiplier associated with the Jacobian of the projective transformation. Finally, constructing moment invariants required a transition from the rational to the polynomial theory. In the work [11], classical S​L​(3,ℝ)SL(3,\mathbb{R})-invariant theory was used to describe polynomial multipoint projective differential invariants and, of particular importance for the present paper, to characterize relative invariants of weight −1-1. Thus, only after this preliminary invariant-theoretic foundation had been established did it become possible to return to the original problem of projective moment invariants.

The aim of this paper is to develop a general theory of polynomial first-order projective differential moment invariants. To this end, we use previously obtained results on relative polynomial invariants of the projective group action on the space of polynomials in first-jet coordinates. In particular, explicit invariants of low moment degrees are obtained, their connection with classical invariant theory of ternary forms is established, and compact representations are provided that are suitable for software computation of invariant image characteristics.

For a twice-differentiable function ff with compact support, consider the differential moments

mα,β,r,s​(f)=∫ℝ2xα​yβ​fxr​fys​f​(x,y)​𝑑x​𝑑y,α,β,r,s∈ℤ≥0.m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s}(f)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}f_{x}^{r}f_{y}^{s}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy,\qquad\alpha,\beta,r,s\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

The corresponding formal moment symbols mα,β,r,sm_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} generate the polynomial algebra

𝒟​𝒫=ℝ⁡[mα,β,r,s].\mathcal{DP}=\mathbb{R}[m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s}].

A projective transformation does not, in general, preserve this algebra: after a change of variables, a polynomial moment kernel may become rational, so the projective group action is not defined on the whole of 𝒟​𝒫\mathcal{DP}. At the same time, the action of its Lie algebra 𝔭​𝔤​𝔩3≃𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{pgl}_{3}\simeq\mathfrak{sl}_{3} is well defined on the formal moment variables and is given by derivations of the algebra 𝒟​𝒫\mathcal{DP}. This allows us to define the algebra of polynomial projective differential moment invariants as

ℳ​ℐ=𝒟​𝒫𝔰​𝔩3,\mathcal{MI}=\mathcal{DP}^{\mathfrak{sl}_{3}},

that is, as the subalgebra of moment polynomials annihilated by all operators of this action.

Classical invariant theory offers two natural approaches to studying such an algebra. The first consists in identifying finite-dimensional 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3}-modules in 𝒟​𝒫\mathcal{DP} and applying standard invariant-theoretic methods to them. This is precisely how the module of ten cubic differential moments will be identified below with the space of ternary cubics; the classical Aronhold invariants SS and TT then directly yield two projective moment invariants. However, this approach requires first finding the appropriate finite-dimensional module and therefore does not by itself lead to a general description of all moment invariants.

The second approach, which is central to this paper, also has its origins in classical invariant theory. Instead of searching directly for invariants in the moment algebra, we pass to a multipoint polynomial representation of the projective group in which the projective transformation law has a simpler algebraic structure. This makes it possible to use the already known description of relative projective invariants and is conceptually similar to the symbolic method of classical invariant theory: compact multipoint kernels are used in place of unwieldy polynomials in moment variables.

Let 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1} denote the space of polynomial relative invariants of weight −1-1 for the diagonal projective action on nn points, and let ℳ​ℐn\mathcal{MI}_{n} denote the space of moment invariants homogeneous of moment degree nn. The main result of this paper states that, for every n≥3n\geq 3, there is an isomorphism

Φn:(𝒫n,−1)Sn→ℳ​ℐn,Φn−1=Poln.\Phi_{n}:(\mathcal{P}_{n,-1})^{S_{n}}\xrightarrow{}\mathcal{MI}_{n},\qquad\Phi_{n}^{-1}=\operatorname{Pol}_{n}.

Here, (𝒫n,−1)Sn(\mathcal{P}_{n,-1})^{S_{n}} denotes the subspace of invariants symmetric under permutations of the nn points. The map Φn\Phi_{n} sends such symmetric invariants to moment polynomials, while complete polarization Poln\operatorname{Pol}_{n} provides the inverse passage to relative invariants.

Thus, constructing polynomial projective differential moment invariants reduces to describing the symmetric part of 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1}. Since the space 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1} itself has already been described, this correspondence provides a constructive method for obtaining moment invariants. At the same time, it allows them to be represented by compact formulas for relative invariants, without expanding the corresponding expressions into polynomials with hundreds or thousands of moment monomials.

The passage from the formal moment algebra to differential moments as integral functionals of ff is justified separately. It is proved that, on the subalgebra containing the constructed invariants, this integral realization is injective, and hence the passage from formal moments to their integral definitions does not produce additional algebraic relations.

Explicit results are obtained for low moment degrees: nonzero invariants of degrees 11 and 22 do not exist, and a complete description of the invariants of degree 33 is obtained in terms of the corresponding symmetric relative projective invariants. The ten cubic differential moments form a module of ternary cubics, so the classical Aronhold invariants SS and TT yield moment invariants of degrees 44 and 66. In particular, SS is proportional to the known invariant Inv2,0\operatorname{Inv}_{2,0} from [5].

We use the following terminology throughout. The principal object is called a projective differential moment invariant; within this paper, we use the abbreviated term moment invariant. For relative invariants depending on several first jets, we use the term multipoint relative projective differential invariant. When the number of points needs to be specified, we call it nn-point; when the context is unambiguous, we abbreviate the term to relative invariant.

A polynomial b⁡(x,y,p,q)b(x,y,p,q) appearing in the integral ∫Ωb⁡(x,y,p,q)​f​(x,y)​𝑑x​𝑑y\int_{\Omega}b(x,y,p,q)f(x,y)\,dx\,dy is called a single-point moment kernel. A polynomial Q⁡(z1,…,zn)Q(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) that defines a moment polynomial through the map Φn\Phi_{n} is called a multipoint moment kernel. We use the abbreviated term kernel when the number of points is clear from the context.

In this paper, we identify the real Lie groups P​G​L​(3,ℝ)PGL(3,\mathbb{R}) and S​L​(3,ℝ)SL(3,\mathbb{R}), as well as their Lie algebras 𝔭​𝔤​𝔩3\mathfrak{pgl}_{3} and 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3}. For the geometric action on the plane, we use the notation P​G​L​(3,ℝ)PGL(3,\mathbb{R}), while for the corresponding linear representations and classical invariants, we use S​L​(3,ℝ)SL(3,\mathbb{R}). We denote the operator action on the formal moment algebra as an action of 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3}.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, the main results are presented in a form suitable for direct use. Section 3 provides the necessary background on the projective action and multipoint relative invariants. Section 4 describes the Lie algebra action on the moment algebra, proves the correspondence theorem, and justifies the passage from the formal moment algebra to its integral realization. Section 5 is devoted to explicit constructions of invariants of low moment degrees, structural properties of the moment algebra, and a description of rational invariants.

2. Main Results

In this section, we present the main invariant constructions in a form suitable for direct use. Proofs of these results and generalizations will be given in the subsequent sections.

2.1. Ternary Cubic

Let f=f⁡(x,y)f=f(x,y) be a twice-differentiable intensity function of a grayscale image. Let Ω=supp⁡f\Omega=\operatorname{supp}f denote the image domain, and, to simplify the subsequent formulas, set

p=fx,q=fy,w=x​p+y​q.p=f_{x},\qquad q=f_{y},\qquad w=xp+yq.

Consider the ten differential moments

μi​j​k=∫Ωpi​qj​(−w)k​f​(x,y)​𝑑x​𝑑y,i+j+k=3,\mu_{ijk}=\int_{\Omega}p^{i}q^{j}(-w)^{k}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy,\qquad i+j+k=3,

which we will regard as the coefficients of a ternary cubic

ℱ⁡(ξ,η,ζ)=μ300​ξ3+μ030​η3+μ003​ζ3+3​μ210​ξ2​η+3​μ120​ξ​η2+3​μ201​ξ2​ζ+3​μ102​ξ​ζ2+3​μ021​η2​ζ+3​μ012​η​ζ2+6​μ111​ξ​η​ζ.\begin{gathered}\mathcal{F}(\xi,\eta,\zeta)=\mu_{300}\xi^{3}+\mu_{030}\eta^{3}+\mu_{003}\zeta^{3}+3\mu_{210}\xi^{2}\eta+3\mu_{120}\xi\eta^{2}+3\mu_{201}\xi^{2}\zeta\\ +3\mu_{102}\xi\zeta^{2}+3\mu_{021}\eta^{2}\zeta+3\mu_{012}\eta\zeta^{2}+6\mu_{111}\xi\eta\zeta.\end{gathered}

Under this identification, the space spanned by the coefficients μi​j​k\mu_{ijk} is a 1010-dimensional S​L​(3,ℝ)SL(3,\mathbb{R})-module dual to the classical module of ternary cubics in the variables ξ,η,ζ\xi,\eta,\zeta. The problem of constructing projective invariants as polynomials in these ten moments reduces to the problem of constructing invariants of a ternary cubic. Thus, it can be solved by directly applying known results from classical invariant theory; see [12]:

Theorem 2.1.

All polynomial invariants of a ternary cubic, viewed as polynomials in μi​j​k\mu_{ijk}, are generated by two algebraically independent invariants of degree 44 and degree 6.6.

Denote these two generating invariants by SS and TT, and, to express them explicitly, set:

A=μ300,B=μ030,C=μ003,D=μ210,E=μ021,\displaystyle A=\mu_{300},\qquad B=\mu_{030},\qquad C=\mu_{003},\qquad D=\mu_{210},\qquad E=\mu_{021},
F=μ102,G=μ120,H=μ012,I=μ201,J=μ111.\displaystyle F=\mu_{102},\qquad G=\mu_{120},\qquad H=\mu_{012},\qquad I=\mu_{201},\qquad J=\mu_{111}.

We use the notation A,B,…,JA,B,\ldots,J as local abbreviations for these moments only in the explicit polynomial formulas for the invariants SS and TT, including the formula in the appendix. Elsewhere in the text, we retain the indexed notation μi​j​k\mu_{ijk}.

The first invariant then takes the form

S=\displaystyle S={} A​G​E​C−A​G​H2−A​J​B​C+A​J​E​H+A​F​B​H−A​F​E2\displaystyle AGEC-AGH^{2}-AJBC+AJEH+AFBH-AFE^{2}
−D2​E​C+D2​H2+D​I​B​C−D​I​E​H+D​G​J​C−D​G​F​H\displaystyle-D^{2}EC+D^{2}H^{2}+DIBC-DIEH+DGJC-DGFH
−2​D​J2​H+3​D​J​F​E−D​F2​B−I2​B​H+I2​E2\displaystyle-2DJ^{2}H+3DJFE-DF^{2}B-I^{2}BH+I^{2}E^{2}

(1) +G2​F2−2​G​J2​F+J4.\displaystyle+G^{2}F^{2}-2GJ^{2}F+J^{4}.

It contains 2525 monomials and is proportional to the invariant Inv2,0\operatorname{Inv}_{2,0} from [5]. The second invariant, TT, contains 103103 monomials; its formula is given in the appendix; see (20).

Thus, the known 25-term expression is one of the two fundamental invariants of this moment module. All other projective moment invariants obtained have substantially more unwieldy explicit expansions in differential moments. Some of the invariants constructed in this paper are implemented in the accompanying software repository, which allows them to be computed without explicitly expanding unwieldy polynomial formulas. Therefore, instead of full formulas, we use their compact symbolic representations, which can, when necessary, be expanded into explicit polynomials in differential moments.

2.2. Projective Moment Invariants of Degree Three

For the full projective group, nonzero moment invariants of degrees 11 and 22 do not exist, and the lowest degree at which new invariants arise is degree 33. To write them compactly, we use three points

zi=(xi,yi,pi,qi),pi=∂xif(xi,yi),qi=∂yif(xi,yi),wi=xipi+yiqi,i=1,2,3,z_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i},p_{i},q_{i}),\quad p_{i}=\partial_{x_{i}}f(x_{i},y_{i}),\quad q_{i}=\partial_{y_{i}}f(x_{i},y_{i}),\quad w_{i}=x_{i}p_{i}+y_{i}q_{i},\qquad i=1,2,3,

Set

ℓi=(pi,qi,−wi),vi=(xi,yi,1).\ell_{i}=(p_{i},q_{i},-w_{i}),\qquad v_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i},1).

For distinct indices i,j,ki,j,k, define

Di​j​k=det(piqi−wipjqj−wjpkqk−wk),Ci​j=ℓi⋅vj=pi​xj+qi​yj−wi.D_{ijk}=\det\begin{pmatrix}p_{i}&q_{i}&-w_{i}\\ p_{j}&q_{j}&-w_{j}\\ p_{k}&q_{k}&-w_{k}\end{pmatrix},\qquad C_{ij}=\ell_{i}\cdot v_{j}=p_{i}x_{j}+q_{i}y_{j}-w_{i}.

In formal expansions in DD-moments, the quantities wiw_{i} are temporarily treated as independent symbols. It is for this form that we subsequently report the number of monomials, the number of DD-moments used, and the DD-order of the representation. When realizing these expressions on first jets, we substitute wi=xi​pi+yi​qiw_{i}=x_{i}p_{i}+y_{i}q_{i}, so that

Ci​j=pi​(xj−xi)+qi​(yj−yi).C_{ij}=p_{i}(x_{j}-x_{i})+q_{i}(y_{j}-y_{i}).

Thus, the independence of the symbols wiw_{i} is merely a convention for the formal expansion; the geometric transformation laws apply after the indicated substitution.

To pass from multipoint moment kernels to moment polynomials, we use the map Φn\Phi_{n}. In terms of DD-moments (see Wang [5]),

ϕα​β​r​s​t=∫Ωxα​yβ​pr​qs​wt​f​(x,y)​𝑑x​𝑑y\phi_{\alpha\beta rst}=\int_{\Omega}x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}p^{r}q^{s}w^{t}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy

Φn​(∏ν=1nxναν​yνβν​pνrν​qνsν​wνtν)=∏ν=1nϕαν​βν​rν​sν​tν\Phi_{n}\left(\prod_{\nu=1}^{n}x_{\nu}^{\alpha_{\nu}}y_{\nu}^{\beta_{\nu}}p_{\nu}^{r_{\nu}}q_{\nu}^{s_{\nu}}w_{\nu}^{t_{\nu}}\right)=\prod_{\nu=1}^{n}\phi_{\alpha_{\nu}\beta_{\nu}r_{\nu}s_{\nu}t_{\nu}}

and on arbitrary multipoint polynomial kernels by linear extension; for example,

Φ3​(x1​p12​y2​q22​p3​q3​w3)=ϕ10200​ϕ01020​ϕ00111.\Phi_{3}(x_{1}p_{1}^{2}\,y_{2}q_{2}^{2}\,p_{3}q_{3}w_{3})=\phi_{10200}\phi_{01020}\phi_{00111}.

Theorem 2.2.

Every invariant I∈ℳ​ℐ3I\in\mathcal{MI}_{3} has the form

I=Φ3​(D123 3​Q​(𝖷,𝖸,𝖹,U,V)),I=\Phi_{3}\left(D_{123}^{\,3}Q(\mathsf{X},\mathsf{Y},\mathsf{Z},U,V)\right),

2.3. General Moment Correspondence

This construction extends to an arbitrary moment degree n≥1n\geq 1.

A polynomial Q⁡(z1,…,zn)Q(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) is called a multipoint relative projective differential invariant of weight −1-1 if the identity

(5) Q⁡(g​z1,…,g​zn)=(∏i=1njg​(xi,yi))−1​Q​(z1,…,zn),Q(gz_{1},\ldots,gz_{n})=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}j_{g}(x_{i},y_{i})\right)^{-1}Q(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}),

holds for every projective transformation gg, where jg​(xi,yi)j_{g}(x_{i},y_{i}) is the signed Jacobian of the projective transformation at the point (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}).

The following main assertion holds.

Theorem 2.4.

Let n≥1n\geq 1, and let Q⁡(z1,…,zn)Q(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) be a symmetric relative projective invariant of weight −1-1. Then Φn​(Q)\Phi_{n}(Q) is a projective differential moment invariant of moment degree nn. Conversely, every projective differential moment invariant II of moment degree nn can be written as I=Φn​(Q),I=\Phi_{n}(Q), where QQ is a symmetric relative projective invariant of weight −1-1 in nn sets of variables.

This theorem establishes a connection between projective moment invariants and symmetric multipoint relative invariants of weight −1-1. A description of such relative invariants in terms of admissible monomials in Di​j​kD_{ijk} and Ci​jC_{ij} is given in Section 3, while the proof of the theorem itself is given in Section 4.

For an admissible pair (g,f)(g,f), let εg=sgn⁡jg​(x,y)\varepsilon_{g}=\operatorname{sgn}j_{g}(x,y) denote the constant sign of the Jacobian on a connected domain containing the support of ff. Then, for every I∈ℳ​ℐnI\in\mathcal{MI}_{n}, we have

I⁡(g⋅f)=εgn​I​(f).I(g\cdot f)=\varepsilon_{g}^{\,n}I(f).

Indeed, let I=Φn​(Q)I=\Phi_{n}(Q), where QQ is a symmetric relative invariant of weight −1-1. A change of variables in the multiple integral and the relative invariance law give

I⁡(g⋅f)\displaystyle I(g\cdot f) =∫ΩnQ⁡(g​z1,…,g​zn)​∏i=1n(|jg​(xi,yi)|​f​(xi,yi)​d​xi​d​yi)\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega^{n}}Q(gz_{1},\ldots,gz_{n})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(|j_{g}(x_{i},y_{i})|f(x_{i},y_{i})\,dx_{i}\,dy_{i}\bigr)
=∫ΩnQ⁡(z1,…,zn)​∏i=1n(|jg​(xi,yi)|jg​(xi,yi)​f​(xi,yi)​d​xi​d​yi)=εgn​I​(f).\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega^{n}}Q(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{|j_{g}(x_{i},y_{i})|}{j_{g}(x_{i},y_{i})}f(x_{i},y_{i})\,dx_{i}\,dy_{i}\right)=\varepsilon_{g}^{\,n}I(f).

Thus, invariants of even moment degree are preserved under all admissible transformations, while invariants of odd degree change sign under orientation reversal and are pseudoinvariants.

In addition to the correspondence theorem, two structural properties of moment invariants are established. First, the space ℳ​ℐ3\mathcal{MI}_{3} is infinite-dimensional, and the algebra ℳ​ℐ\mathcal{MI} is not finitely generated. Thus, finite generation of each module 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1} over the algebra of absolute invariants 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n} for fixed n≥3n\geq 3 does not imply finite generation of the algebra of all moment invariants.

Second, every rational moment invariant can be written in the form

PQ,P,Q∈ℳ​ℐ,Q≠0.\frac{P}{Q},\qquad P,Q\in\mathcal{MI},\quad Q\neq 0.

Thus, the field of rational moment invariants is the field of fractions of the algebra ℳ​ℐ\mathcal{MI}. Proofs of both results are given in Section 5.

3. Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce the projective group action on the image coordinates and its first derivatives, the basic constructions Di​j​kD_{ijk} and Ci​jC_{ij}, and their transformation laws, which will subsequently be used to construct projective differential moment invariants.

3.1. The projective group and its action

A projective transformation of the plane is determined, up to a nonzero scalar factor, by a real nonsingular matrix

H=(a1a2a3b1b2b3c1c2c3)∈G​L​(3,ℝ).H=\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}&a_{2}&a_{3}\\ b_{1}&b_{2}&b_{3}\\ c_{1}&c_{2}&c_{3}\end{pmatrix}\in GL(3,\mathbb{R}).

Let g=[H]∈P​G​L​(3,ℝ)g=[H]\in PGL(3,\mathbb{R}) denote the corresponding equivalence class of the matrix. In an affine chart, the coordinate map hgh_{g} takes the form

hg​(x,y)=(x~,y~)=(a1​x+a2​y+a3s,b1​x+b2​y+b3s),s=c1​x+c2​y+c3,h_{g}(x,y)=(\widetilde{x},\widetilde{y})=\left(\frac{a_{1}x+a_{2}y+a_{3}}{s},\frac{b_{1}x+b_{2}y+b_{3}}{s}\right),\qquad s=c_{1}x+c_{2}y+c_{3},

and is defined whenever s≠0s\neq 0. Its signed Jacobian is

jg​(x,y)=detD​hg​(x,y)=detHs3.j_{g}(x,y)=\det Dh_{g}(x,y)=\frac{\det H}{s^{3}}.

All such transformations form a group called the projective group of the plane, P​G​L​(3,ℝ)PGL(3,\mathbb{R}). Following the convention adopted in the introduction, we identify this group with S​L​(3,ℝ)SL(3,\mathbb{R}) and its Lie algebra with 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3}.

In applications, the normalization c3=1c_{3}=1 is often used. Since it is not available for every transformation, and the corresponding matrix representatives are not closed under multiplication, we do not impose it hereafter.

We describe an image by a real-valued intensity function f=f⁡(x,y)f=f(x,y). We assume that it is twice differentiable on its domain and vanishes outside it. The support of the function, that is, the closure of the set of points where f⁡(x,y)≠0f(x,y)\neq 0, will be denoted by Ω\Omega.

A projective transformation cannot be applied to every image: its denominator s=c1​x+c2​y+c3s=c_{1}x+c_{2}y+c_{3} may vanish on the support of the function ff. A pair (g,f)(g,f) consisting of a projective transformation gg and an image ff to which it is applied will be called admissible if there exists an open connected domain UU containing the entire support Ω\Omega of the image and on which s≠0s\neq 0. Under this condition, the transformation is defined throughout UU, and its Jacobian has a constant nonzero sign there. Thus, we distinguish the signed Jacobian in the transformation laws of algebraic kernels from its absolute value in the change-of-variables formula.

For an admissible pair (g,f)(g,f), we define the action of the projective transformation on the image by

(g⋅f)​(hg​(x,y))=f⁡(x,y),(x,y)∈U.(g\cdot f)\bigl(h_{g}(x,y)\bigr)=f(x,y),\qquad(x,y)\in U.

Thus, on hg​(U)h_{g}(U), we have

g⋅f=f∘hg−1,g\cdot f=f\circ h_{g}^{-1},

and outside this domain, we extend the function g⋅fg\cdot f by zero.

The transformation law of a moment invariant under the projective group action depends on its moment degree and the sign of the Jacobian, as specified by the following assertion.

Theorem 3.1.

Let (g,f)(g,f) be an admissible pair, and let

εg=sgn⁡jg​(x,y),(x,y)∈U,\varepsilon_{g}=\operatorname{sgn}j_{g}(x,y),\qquad(x,y)\in U,

be the constant sign of the Jacobian on the domain UU. Then, for every I∈ℳ​ℐnI\in\mathcal{MI}_{n}, we have

I⁡(g⋅f)=εgn​I​(f).I(g\cdot f)=\varepsilon_{g}^{\,n}I(f).
Proof.

Let I=Φn​(Q)I=\Phi_{n}(Q), where QQ is a symmetric relative invariant of weight −1-1. A change of variables in the multiple integral and the relative invariance law give

I⁡(g⋅f)\displaystyle I(g\cdot f) =∫ΩnQ⁡(g​z1,…,g​zn)​∏i=1n(|jg​(xi,yi)|​f​(xi,yi)​d​xi​d​yi)=\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega^{n}}Q(gz_{1},\ldots,gz_{n})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(|j_{g}(x_{i},y_{i})|f(x_{i},y_{i})\,dx_{i}\,dy_{i}\bigr)=
=∫ΩnQ⁡(z1,…,zn)​∏i=1n(|jg​(xi,yi)|jg​(xi,yi)​f​(xi,yi)​d​xi​d​yi)=εgn​I​(f).\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega^{n}}Q(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{|j_{g}(x_{i},y_{i})|}{j_{g}(x_{i},y_{i})}f(x_{i},y_{i})\,dx_{i}\,dy_{i}\right)=\varepsilon_{g}^{\,n}I(f).

∎

Thus, invariants of even moment degree are preserved under all admissible transformations, while invariants of odd moment degree change sign under orientation reversal and are pseudoinvariants.

The projective group action is naturally prolonged to first derivatives:

(6) p⟼p~=sdetH​[−(b1​c2−b2​c1)​(p​x+q​y)+(b2​c3−b3​c2)​p−(b1​c3−b3​c1)​q],q⟼q~=sdetH​[(a1​c2−a2​c1)​(p​x+q​y)−(a2​c3−a3​c2)​p+(a1​c3−a3​c1)​q],\begin{gathered}p\longmapsto\widetilde{p}=\frac{s}{\det H}\Bigl[-(b_{1}c_{2}-b_{2}c_{1})(px+qy)+(b_{2}c_{3}-b_{3}c_{2})p-(b_{1}c_{3}-b_{3}c_{1})q\Bigr],\\ q\longmapsto\widetilde{q}=\frac{s}{\det H}\Bigl[(a_{1}c_{2}-a_{2}c_{1})(px+qy)-(a_{2}c_{3}-a_{3}c_{2})p+(a_{1}c_{3}-a_{3}c_{1})q\Bigr],\end{gathered}

see, for example, [9].

3.2. Diagonal action

Consider nn independent sets of variables zi=(xi,yi,pi,qi)z_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i},p_{i},q_{i}), i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, and denote the corresponding partial derivatives by pi=fx​(xi,yi)p_{i}=f_{x}(x_{i},y_{i}) and qi=fy​(xi,yi)q_{i}=f_{y}(x_{i},y_{i}).

The diagonal action means that the same element g=[H]g=[H] acts on each set ziz_{i}. In particular,

(xi,yi)⟼(x~i,y~i)=(a1​xi+a2​yi+a3si,b1​xi+b2​yi+b3si),si=c1​xi+c2​yi+c3,(x_{i},y_{i})\longmapsto(\widetilde{x}_{i},\widetilde{y}_{i})=\left(\frac{a_{1}x_{i}+a_{2}y_{i}+a_{3}}{s_{i}},\frac{b_{1}x_{i}+b_{2}y_{i}+b_{3}}{s_{i}}\right),\qquad s_{i}=c_{1}x_{i}+c_{2}y_{i}+c_{3},

and the formulas for pi,qip_{i},q_{i} are obtained from (6) by replacing (x,y,p,q,s)(x,y,p,q,s) with (xi,yi,pi,qi,si)(x_{i},y_{i},p_{i},q_{i},s_{i}).

We denote the coordinate Jacobian multiplier of the diagonal action by

𝒥g​(𝒛)=∏i=1njg​(xi,yi)=(detH)n∏i=1nsi3,𝒛=(z1,…,zn).\mathcal{J}_{g}(\boldsymbol{z})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}j_{g}(x_{i},y_{i})=\frac{(\det H)^{n}}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}s_{i}^{3}},\qquad\boldsymbol{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}).

It accounts for the change of coordinates (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) and is used in the relative invariance laws. The change-of-variables formula for integrals uses its absolute value

|𝒥g​(𝒛)|=∏i=1n|jg​(xi,yi)|.|\mathcal{J}_{g}(\boldsymbol{z})|=\prod_{i=1}^{n}|j_{g}(x_{i},y_{i})|.

For the prolonged action on all 4​n4n variables ziz_{i}, the determinant of the Jacobian matrix equals 11.

3.3. Relative and absolute invariants

Let Rn=ℝ⁡[𝒛]R_{n}=\mathbb{R}[\boldsymbol{z}] denote the polynomial ring, and let Kn=Frac⁡(Rn)K_{n}=\operatorname{Frac}(R_{n}) denote its field of fractions. Projective substitutions are rational: they are defined in KnK_{n} but generally do not preserve RnR_{n}. A rational function F∈KnF\in K_{n} is called a multipoint relative projective differential invariant of weight ω\omega if the identity

F⁡(g​𝒛)=𝒥g​(𝒛)ω​F​(𝒛).F(g\boldsymbol{z})=\mathcal{J}_{g}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\omega}F(\boldsymbol{z}).

holds for all g∈P​G​L​(3,ℝ)g\in PGL(3,\mathbb{R}). Hereafter, it suffices to consider integer weights ω∈ℤ\omega\in\mathbb{Z}, in particular ω=0\omega=0 and ω=−1\omega=-1. Invariants of weight 00 are called absolute.

We denote by 𝒫n,ω⊂Rn\mathcal{P}_{n,\omega}\subset R_{n} the vector space of polynomial relative invariants of weight ω\omega, and by 𝒜n=𝒫n,0\mathcal{A}_{n}=\mathcal{P}_{n,0} the algebra of absolute polynomial invariants. For each ω\omega, the space 𝒫n,ω\mathcal{P}_{n,\omega} is a module over 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n}.

Polynomial absolute invariants and modules of relative invariants were studied in [11]. We recall the results needed to describe 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1}. The determinants Di​j​kD_{ijk} and the quantities Ci​jC_{ij}, introduced in Subsection 2.2, satisfy the transformation laws

Di​j​k⟼si​sj​skdetH​Di​j​k,Ci​j⟼sisj​Ci​j.D_{ijk}\longmapsto\frac{s_{i}s_{j}s_{k}}{\det H}D_{ijk},\qquad C_{ij}\longmapsto\frac{s_{i}}{s_{j}}C_{ij}.

For a cycle γ=(i1​i2​…​ir)\gamma=(i_{1}\,i_{2}\,\ldots\,i_{r}), r≥2r\geq 2, in the symmetric group SnS_{n}, define the cyclic invariant

Zγ=Ci1​i2Ci2​i3⋯Cir−1​irCir​i1.Z_{\gamma}=C_{i_{1}i_{2}}C_{i_{2}i_{3}}\cdots C_{i_{r-1}i_{r}}C_{i_{r}i_{1}}.
Theorem 3.2 ([11], Theorem 2.2).

For every n≥3n\geq 3, the algebra 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n} is generated by cyclic invariants:

𝒜n=ℝ⁡[Zγ∣γ∈Sn​ — a cycle of length ​r≥2].\mathcal{A}_{n}=\mathbb{R}\bigl[Z_{\gamma}\mid\gamma\in S_{n}\text{ --- a cycle of length }r\geq 2\bigr].

To describe 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1}, consider the set 𝒯n={I⊂[n]∣|I|=3}\mathcal{T}_{n}=\{I\subset[n]\mid|I|=3\}, where [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}, and, for I={i,j,k}I=\{i,j,k\} with i<j<ki<j<k, set DI=Di​j​kD_{I}=D_{ijk}.

Consider a vector of length (n3)\binom{n}{3}

𝒃=(bI)I∈𝒯n,bI∈ℤ≥0,\boldsymbol{b}=(b_{I})_{I\in\mathcal{T}_{n}},\qquad b_{I}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},

and a nonnegative integer n×nn\times n matrix with zero diagonal

𝒂=(ai​j),ai​j∈ℤ≥0.\boldsymbol{a}=(a_{ij}),\qquad a_{ij}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

Define the monomial

(7) P𝒃,𝒂=∏I∈𝒯nDIbI​∏i≠jCi​jai​j.P_{\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{a}}=\prod_{I\in\mathcal{T}_{n}}D_{I}^{b_{I}}\prod_{i\neq j}C_{ij}^{a_{ij}}.

Its CC-degree is defined as the number ∑i≠jai​j\sum_{i\neq j}a_{ij}. For each ii, set

d𝒃​(i)=∑I∋ibI,∂𝒂(i)=∑j≠iai​j−∑j≠iaj​i.d_{\boldsymbol{b}}(i)=\sum_{I\ni i}b_{I},\qquad\partial_{\boldsymbol{a}}(i)=\sum_{j\neq i}a_{ij}-\sum_{j\neq i}a_{ji}.

The first quantity accounts for the total multiplicity of occurrences of the index ii in the determinants, while the second gives the balance of its occurrences in the factors Ci​jC_{ij}. The monomial (7) is called admissible if

(8) ∑I∈𝒯nbI=n,d𝒃(i)+∂𝒂(i)=3,i=1,…,n.\sum_{I\in\mathcal{T}_{n}}b_{I}=n,\qquad d_{\boldsymbol{b}}(i)+\partial_{\boldsymbol{a}}(i)=3,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.

The following structural result holds.

Theorem 3.3 ([11], Theorem 3.2).

For every n≥3n\geq 3, the vector space 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1} is spanned by the admissible monomials P𝐛,𝐚P_{\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{a}}.

Since multiplying a relative invariant of weight −1-1 by an absolute invariant does not change its weight, the space 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1} is naturally a module over the algebra 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n}. The following result holds for this module.

Theorem 3.4 ([11], Theorem 4.2).

For every n≥3n\geq 3, the module 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1} is finitely generated over 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n}. A finite generating system can be chosen among the admissible monomials.

4. Projective Differential Moment Invariants

In this section, we pass from the multipoint projective constructions introduced above to differential moments of an image. We first define the corresponding moment variables and the map that sends multipoint polynomial kernels to polynomials in moments. We then state and prove the main result establishing a correspondence between relative projective invariants of weight −1-1 and projective differential moment invariants.

4.1. Differential moments

The differential moments of an image ff are defined as the quantities

(9) mα,β,r,s​(f)=∫Ωxα​yβ​pr​qs​f​(x,y)​𝑑x​𝑑y,α,β,r,s∈ℤ≥0.m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s}(f)=\int_{\Omega}x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}p^{r}q^{s}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy,\qquad\alpha,\beta,r,s\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

Hereafter, we distinguish the following characteristics:

  • •

    moment degree — the total polynomial degree in the moment variables; a moment monomial of degree nn contains nn moment factors, counted with their multiplicities;

  • •

    moment order of mα,β,r,sm_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} — the number α+β+r+s\alpha+\beta+r+s;

  • •

    DD-order of a moment ϕα​β​r​s​t\phi_{\alpha\beta rst} — the number α+β+r+s+t\alpha+\beta+r+s+t, while the DD-order of a particular representation is the maximum of these numbers over its moment factors;

  • •

    differential order — the highest order of derivatives of the function ff used in the kernel; only first derivatives are used in this paper;

  • •

    derivative degree of an individual moment kernel — its polynomial degree in p,qp,q: r+sr+s for mα,β,r,sm_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} and r+s+tr+s+t for ϕα​β​r​s​t\phi_{\alpha\beta rst} after substituting w=x​p+y​qw=xp+yq.

For example, the invariant SS has moment degree 44 and the displayed DD-moment representation has order 33. Each of its moment factors has derivative degree 33, although only derivatives of first differential order are used.

We denote the corresponding single-point moment kernel by bα,β,r,s​(z)=xα​yβ​pr​qsb_{\alpha,\beta,r,s}(z)=x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}p^{r}q^{s}, where z=(x,y,p,q)z=(x,y,p,q).

For an admissible pair (g,f)(g,f), a change of variables gives

mα,β,r,s​(g⋅f)=∫Ωbα,β,r,s​(g​z)​|jg​(x,y)|​f​(x,y)​𝑑x​𝑑y.m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s}(g\cdot f)=\int_{\Omega}b_{\alpha,\beta,r,s}(gz)\,|j_{g}(x,y)|\,f(x,y)\,dx\,dy.

Since the kernel generally becomes rational after a projective transformation, the transformed moment need not be expressible polynomially in terms of the original moments. In contrast, the Lie algebra action of the projective group has a substantially simpler structure: it sends each moment to a linear combination of moments.

Consider the formal algebra

𝒟𝒫=ℝ[mα,β,r,s∣α,β,r,s∈ℤ≥0],\mathcal{DP}=\mathbb{R}[m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s}\mid\alpha,\beta,r,s\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}],

where the moment symbols mα,β,r,sm_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} are algebraically independent variables. We denote by 𝒟​𝒫n\mathcal{DP}_{n} the homogeneous component of degree nn in 𝒟​𝒫\mathcal{DP}. The algebra 𝒟​𝒫\mathcal{DP} is the principal algebraic object in which we will study projective differential moment invariants. The formal approach allows us to study the Lie algebra action on the moment variables instead of considering the projective group action directly.

For a specific image ff, we replace each formal moment symbol mα,β,r,sm_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} with the numerical value of the corresponding differential moment defined by formula (9). This substitution defines a homomorphism evf:𝒟​𝒫→ℝ.\operatorname{ev}_{f}:\mathcal{DP}\to\mathbb{R}. Thus, if I∈𝒟​𝒫I\in\mathcal{DP} is a polynomial in the moment symbols, substituting the moments of the image ff gives the number

I⁡(f)=evf⁡(I).I(f)=\operatorname{ev}_{f}(I).

Similarly, for all 𝒟k=𝒟Xk\mathscr{D}_{k}=\mathscr{D}_{X_{k}}, we obtain

(11) 𝒟1​mα,β,r,s\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{1}m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} =α​mα−1,β,r,s,\displaystyle=\alpha m_{\alpha-1,\beta,r,s},
𝒟2​mα,β,r,s\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{2}m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} =β​mα,β−1,r,s,\displaystyle=\beta m_{\alpha,\beta-1,r,s},
𝒟3​mα,β,r,s\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{3}m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} =(α−r+1)​mα,β,r,s,\displaystyle=(\alpha-r+1)m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s},
𝒟4​mα,β,r,s\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{4}m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} =(β−s+1)​mα,β,r,s,\displaystyle=(\beta-s+1)m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s},
𝒟5​mα,β,r,s\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{5}m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} =α​mα−1,β+1,r,s−s​mα,β,r+1,s−1,\displaystyle=\alpha m_{\alpha-1,\beta+1,r,s}-s\,m_{\alpha,\beta,r+1,s-1},
𝒟6​mα,β,r,s\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{6}m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} =β​mα+1,β−1,r,s−r​mα,β,r−1,s+1,\displaystyle=\beta m_{\alpha+1,\beta-1,r,s}-r\,m_{\alpha,\beta,r-1,s+1},
𝒟7​mα,β,r,s\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{7}m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} =(α+β−2​r−s+3)​mα+1,β,r,s−r​mα,β+1,r−1,s+1,\displaystyle=(\alpha+\beta-2r-s+3)m_{\alpha+1,\beta,r,s}-r\,m_{\alpha,\beta+1,r-1,s+1},
𝒟8​mα,β,r,s\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{8}m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} =(α+β−r−2​s+3)​mα,β+1,r,s−s​mα+1,β,r+1,s−1.\displaystyle=(\alpha+\beta-r-2s+3)m_{\alpha,\beta+1,r,s}-s\,m_{\alpha+1,\beta,r+1,s-1}.

Terms with zero coefficients are omitted, so moments with negative indices do not arise.

The explicit formulas show that the action of 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3} on the moment algebra is compatible with two natural graded structures. In particular, it does not change the number of moment factors in a polynomial and, as follows from (11), preserves the total derivative degree r+sr+s of each moment generator.

A polynomial I∈𝒟​𝒫I\in\mathcal{DP} is called a projective differential moment invariant if it is invariant under the specified action of the Lie algebra 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3}, that is,

𝒟kI=0,k=1,…,8.\mathscr{D}_{k}I=0,\qquad k=1,\ldots,8.

The set of all projective differential moment invariants forms the subalgebra

ℳ​ℐ=𝒟​𝒫𝔰​𝔩3=⋂k=18ker⁡𝒟k.\mathcal{MI}=\mathcal{DP}^{\mathfrak{sl}_{3}}=\bigcap_{k=1}^{8}\ker\mathscr{D}_{k}.

We denote its homogeneous component of moment degree nn by ℳ​ℐn=ℳ​ℐ∩𝒟​𝒫n.\mathcal{MI}_{n}=\mathcal{MI}\cap\mathcal{DP}_{n}.

Formally, the problem of constructing moment invariants now reduces to finding common solutions of the system of linear first-order differential equations (11). The method of characteristics can provide a local description of such solutions in terms of orbit invariants of the corresponding Lie algebra action; however, by itself, it does not provide a general description of those solutions that are polynomials in differential moments. Therefore, below, we use an algebraic approach based on the map Φn\Phi_{n}, polarization, and multipoint relative projective invariants.

4.3. Moment realization and polarization

Every monomial in RnR_{n} has the form

∏i=1nbαi,βi,ri,si​(zi).\prod_{i=1}^{n}b_{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i},r_{i},s_{i}}(z_{i}).

Define the linear map Φn:Rn→𝒟​𝒫n\Phi_{n}:R_{n}\to\mathcal{DP}_{n} by the rule

Φn​(∏i=1nbαi,βi,ri,si​(zi))=∏i=1nmαi,βi,ri,si.\Phi_{n}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}b_{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i},r_{i},s_{i}}(z_{i})\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}m_{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i},r_{i},s_{i}}.

After substituting the moments of an image, it is realized by the multiple integral

(12) Φn​(F)​(f)=∫ΩnF⁡(𝒛)​∏i=1n(f⁡(xi,yi)​d​xi​d​yi).\Phi_{n}(F)(f)=\int_{\Omega^{n}}F(\boldsymbol{z})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(f(x_{i},y_{i})\,dx_{i}\,dy_{i}\bigr).

By the definition of Φn\Phi_{n}, each factor depending on the set of variables ziz_{i} is replaced by the corresponding moment variable. Thus, permuting the sets z1,…,znz_{1},\ldots,z_{n} only permutes the moment factors, leaving their product unchanged. Therefore, for the symmetrization operator

Symn⁡F=1n!​∑σ∈SnF⁡(zσ⁡(1),…,zσ⁡(n)),\operatorname{Sym}_{n}F=\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}F(z_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,z_{\sigma(n)}),

we have

Φn​(F)=Φn​(Symn⁡F).\Phi_{n}(F)=\Phi_{n}(\operatorname{Sym}_{n}F).

For a moment monomial M=∏i=1nmαi,βi,ri,siM=\prod_{i=1}^{n}m_{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i},r_{i},s_{i}}, define its complete polarization by

Poln⁡(M)=1n!​∑σ∈Sn∏i=1nbαi,βi,ri,si​(zσ⁡(i)).\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(M)=\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}b_{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i},r_{i},s_{i}}(z_{\sigma(i)}).

Linear extension gives the map Poln:𝒟​𝒫n→RnSn,\operatorname{Pol}_{n}:\mathcal{DP}_{n}\to R_{n}^{S_{n}}, where RnSnR_{n}^{S_{n}} denotes the subspace of polynomials in RnR_{n} invariant under permutations of the nn sets of variables z1,…,znz_{1},\ldots,z_{n}.

Example 4.2.

For F=x1​y1​p1​q1∈RnF=x_{1}y_{1}p_{1}q_{1}\in R_{n}, we have Φn​(F)=m1,1,1,1​m0,0,0,0n−1\Phi_{n}(F)=m_{1,1,1,1}m_{0,0,0,0}^{\,n-1}, with

Poln⁡(m1,1,1,1​m0,0,0,0n−1)=1n​∑i=1nxi​yi​pi​qi.\operatorname{Pol}_{n}\left(m_{1,1,1,1}m_{0,0,0,0}^{\,n-1}\right)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}p_{i}q_{i}.

Thus, polarization recovers the symmetric preimage of a moment polynomial in the space of polynomials in first-jet coordinates. △\triangle

For each basis element XkX_{k}, k=1,…,8k=1,\ldots,8, we retain the notation ℒk=ℒXk\mathscr{L}_{k}=\mathscr{L}_{X_{k}} for the operator acting on polynomials in the coordinates of a single first jet z=(x,y,p,q)z=(x,y,p,q). We denote by ℒk(i)\mathscr{L}_{k}^{(i)} the same operator acting only on the variables zi=(xi,yi,pi,qi)z_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i},p_{i},q_{i}), that is, the operator obtained from ℒk\mathscr{L}_{k} by the substitution (x,y,p,q)⟼(xi,yi,pi,qi).(x,y,p,q)\longmapsto(x_{i},y_{i},p_{i},q_{i}). Then the operator of the diagonal action on nn sets of variables takes the form

ℒk[n]=∑i=1nℒk(i),k=1,…,8.\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathscr{L}_{k}^{(i)},\qquad k=1,\ldots,8.

The maps Φn\Phi_{n} and Poln\operatorname{Pol}_{n} not only relate multipoint kernels to moment polynomials but are also compatible with the action of the Lie algebra 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3}, as formalized in the following lemma.

Lemma 4.1.

For every n≥1n\geq 1, the following identities hold:

(13) Φn∘Poln\displaystyle\Phi_{n}\circ\operatorname{Pol}_{n} =id𝒟​𝒫n,\displaystyle=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal{DP}_{n}},
(14) Poln∘Φn\displaystyle\operatorname{Pol}_{n}\circ\Phi_{n} =Symn.\displaystyle=\operatorname{Sym}_{n}.

Moreover, for every k=1,…,8k=1,\ldots,8, F∈RnF\in R_{n}, and I∈𝒟​𝒫nI\in\mathcal{DP}_{n}, we have

(15) 𝒟k​Φn​(F)\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{k}\Phi_{n}(F) =Φn​(ℒk[n]​F),\displaystyle=\Phi_{n}(\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F),
Poln⁡(𝒟k​I)\displaystyle\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(\mathscr{D}_{k}I) =ℒk[n]​Poln⁡(I).\displaystyle=\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(I).

In particular, Φn\Phi_{n} and Poln\operatorname{Pol}_{n} are mutually inverse maps between RnSnR_{n}^{S_{n}} and 𝒟​𝒫n\mathcal{DP}_{n} and intertwine the corresponding actions of the Lie algebra 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3}.

Proof.

All maps in these identities are linear, so it suffices to verify them on monomials.

Let bi=bαi,βi,ri,sib_{i}=b_{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i},r_{i},s_{i}}, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, be single-point moment kernels of monomial form, and let

M=∏i=1nmbiM=\prod_{i=1}^{n}m_{b_{i}}

be the corresponding moment monomial. By the definition of polarization,

Poln⁡(M)=1n!​∑σ∈Sn∏i=1nbi​(zσ⁡(i)).\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(M)=\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}(z_{\sigma(i)}).

For every permutation σ∈Sn\sigma\in S_{n}, applying Φn\Phi_{n} replaces the factors bi​(zσ⁡(i))b_{i}(z_{\sigma(i)}) with the corresponding moments mbim_{b_{i}}, so

Φn​(∏i=1nbi​(zσ⁡(i)))=∏i=1nmbi=M.\Phi_{n}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}(z_{\sigma(i)})\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}m_{b_{i}}=M.

Hence,

Φn​(Poln⁡(M))=1n!​∑σ∈SnM=M,\Phi_{n}(\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(M))=\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}M=M,

which proves (13). Now let

F=∏i=1nbi​(zi)∈Rn.F=\prod_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}(z_{i})\in R_{n}.

Then Φn​(F)=M\Phi_{n}(F)=M, and therefore

Poln⁡(Φn​(F))=1n!​∑σ∈Sn∏i=1nbi​(zσ⁡(i))=Symn⁡F.\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(\Phi_{n}(F))=\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}(z_{\sigma(i)})=\operatorname{Sym}_{n}F.

By linearity, we obtain (14) for arbitrary F∈RnF\in R_{n}. In particular, if FF is symmetric, then Symn⁡F=F\operatorname{Sym}_{n}F=F, which implies that Φn\Phi_{n} and Poln\operatorname{Pol}_{n} are mutually inverse on RnSnR_{n}^{S_{n}} and 𝒟​𝒫n\mathcal{DP}_{n}.

We now verify the first identity in (15). We have

ℒk[n]​F=∑i=1n(ℒk​bi)​(zi)​∏j≠ibj​(zj).\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\mathscr{L}_{k}b_{i})(z_{i})\prod_{j\neq i}b_{j}(z_{j}).

Applying Φn\Phi_{n} and using the definition of Φ1\Phi_{1}, we obtain

Φn​(ℒk[n]​F)=∑i=1nΦ1​(ℒk​bi)​∏j≠imbj.\Phi_{n}(\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Phi_{1}(\mathscr{L}_{k}b_{i})\prod_{j\neq i}m_{b_{j}}.

On the other hand, by definition, 𝒟k​mbi=Φ1​(ℒk​bi),\mathscr{D}_{k}m_{b_{i}}=\Phi_{1}(\mathscr{L}_{k}b_{i}), and 𝒟k\mathscr{D}_{k} acts on 𝒟​𝒫\mathcal{DP} as a derivation. Therefore,

𝒟k​Φn​(F)=𝒟k​(∏i=1nmbi)=∑i=1nΦ1​(ℒk​bi)​∏j≠imbj=Φn​(ℒk[n]​F).\mathscr{D}_{k}\Phi_{n}(F)=\mathscr{D}_{k}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}m_{b_{i}}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Phi_{1}(\mathscr{L}_{k}b_{i})\prod_{j\neq i}m_{b_{j}}=\Phi_{n}(\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F).

Linearity gives the first equality in (15) for arbitrary F∈RnF\in R_{n}.

For the second equality, observe that the operator ℒk[n]\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]} commutes with permutations of the sets of variables and hence with the operator Symn\operatorname{Sym}_{n}. Let I∈𝒟​𝒫nI\in\mathcal{DP}_{n} and F=Poln⁡(I).F=\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(I). Then FF is symmetric and, by (13), Φn​(F)=I\Phi_{n}(F)=I. Thus,

Poln⁡(𝒟k​I)\displaystyle\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(\mathscr{D}_{k}I) =Poln⁡(𝒟k​Φn​(F))=Poln⁡(Φn​(ℒk[n]​F))=Symn⁡(ℒk[n]​F)=ℒk[n]​Symn​F=\displaystyle=\operatorname{Pol}_{n}\bigl(\mathscr{D}_{k}\Phi_{n}(F)\bigr)=\operatorname{Pol}_{n}\bigl(\Phi_{n}(\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F)\bigr)=\operatorname{Sym}_{n}(\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F)=\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}\operatorname{Sym}_{n}F=
=ℒk[n]​F=ℒk[n]​Poln⁡(I).\displaystyle=\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F=\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(I).

This proves the second equality and completes the proof of the lemma.

∎

4.4. Completeness theorem

We first establish a connection between the group law of relative invariance and the conditions of annihilation by the corresponding Lie algebra operators. For a polynomial kernel FF, the weight −1-1 condition is written as 𝒥g​(𝒛)​F​(g​𝒛)=F⁡(𝒛).\mathcal{J}_{g}(\boldsymbol{z})F(g\boldsymbol{z})=F(\boldsymbol{z}). Differentiating this equality along the one-parameter subgroups generated by the basis elements XkX_{k} gives the system

(16) ℒk[n]F=0,k=1,…,8.\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F=0,\qquad k=1,\ldots,8.

Conversely, suppose that (16) holds. For the one-parameter subgroup gt=exp⁡(t​Xk)g_{t}=\exp(tX_{k}), differentiating the coordinate Jacobian multiplier 𝒥gt\mathcal{J}_{g_{t}} and applying the chain rule gives

dd​t​[𝒥gt​(𝒛)​F​(gt​𝒛)]=𝒥gt​(𝒛)​(ℒk[n]​F)​(gt​𝒛)=0.\frac{d}{dt}\left[\mathcal{J}_{g_{t}}(\boldsymbol{z})F(g_{t}\boldsymbol{z})\right]=\mathcal{J}_{g_{t}}(\boldsymbol{z})\bigl(\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F\bigr)(g_{t}\boldsymbol{z})=0.

At t=0t=0, the expression in square brackets equals F⁡(𝒛)F(\boldsymbol{z}), and hence 𝒥gt​(𝒛)​F​(gt​𝒛)=F⁡(𝒛)\mathcal{J}_{g_{t}}(\boldsymbol{z})F(g_{t}\boldsymbol{z})=F(\boldsymbol{z}) for each of these one-parameter subgroups. By the multiplication rule for Jacobians, the same equality holds for their compositions. Since X1,…,X8X_{1},\ldots,X_{8} form a basis of 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3} and the connected group P​G​L​(3,ℝ)≃S​L​(3,ℝ)PGL(3,\mathbb{R})\simeq SL(3,\mathbb{R}) is generated by its one-parameter subgroups, the relative invariance law holds for all g∈P​G​L​(3,ℝ)g\in PGL(3,\mathbb{R}).

Thus,

(17) F∈𝒫n,−1⟺ℒk[n]F=0for k=1,…,8.F\in\mathcal{P}_{n,-1}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F=0\quad\text{for }k=1,\ldots,8.

This characterization of relative invariants, together with the intertwining property of the Lie algebra actions, now allows us to establish an exact correspondence between multipoint kernels of weight −1-1 and projective differential moment invariants.

Theorem 4.1.

For every n≥1n\geq 1, the map Φn\Phi_{n} sends 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1} to ℳ​ℐn\mathcal{MI}_{n}. Its restriction

Φn:(𝒫n,−1)Sn⟶ℳ​ℐn\Phi_{n}:(\mathcal{P}_{n,-1})^{S_{n}}\longrightarrow\mathcal{MI}_{n}

is an isomorphism of vector spaces whose inverse is the complete polarization operator Poln\operatorname{Pol}_{n}.

Proof.

First, let F∈𝒫n,−1F\in\mathcal{P}_{n,-1}. By (17), we have ℒk[n]F=0,k=1,…,8.\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F=0,k=1,\ldots,8. By Lemma 4.1, the map Φn\Phi_{n} intertwines the corresponding Lie algebra actions, so

𝒟kΦn(F)=Φn(ℒk[n]F)=0,k=1,…,8.\mathscr{D}_{k}\Phi_{n}(F)=\Phi_{n}(\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F)=0,\qquad k=1,\ldots,8.

Since Φn​(F)∈𝒟​𝒫n\Phi_{n}(F)\in\mathcal{DP}_{n}, the definition of a moment invariant implies that Φn​(F)∈ℳ​ℐn.\Phi_{n}(F)\in\mathcal{MI}_{n}. Thus, in particular, the restriction of Φn\Phi_{n} to (𝒫n,−1)Sn(\mathcal{P}_{n,-1})^{S_{n}} is well defined.

Now let I∈ℳ​ℐnI\in\mathcal{MI}_{n} and F=Poln⁡(I).F=\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(I). By the definition of polarization, FF is a symmetric polynomial. Moreover,

𝒟kI=0,k=1,…,8.\mathscr{D}_{k}I=0,\qquad k=1,\ldots,8.

Using Lemma 4.1 again, we obtain

ℒk[n]F=ℒk[n]Poln(I)=Poln(𝒟kI)=0,k=1,…,8.\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F=\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(I)=\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(\mathscr{D}_{k}I)=0,\qquad k=1,\ldots,8.

By (17), this means that F∈𝒫n,−1F\in\mathcal{P}_{n,-1}. Hence,

Poln⁡(I)∈(𝒫n,−1)Sn.\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(I)\in(\mathcal{P}_{n,-1})^{S_{n}}.

It remains to verify that the maps are mutually inverse. By Lemma 4.1, for every I∈ℳ​ℐnI\in\mathcal{MI}_{n}, we have Φn​(Poln⁡(I))=I.\Phi_{n}(\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(I))=I. Therefore, Φn\Phi_{n} is surjective onto ℳ​ℐn\mathcal{MI}_{n}. For symmetric F∈𝒫n,−1F\in\mathcal{P}_{n,-1}, the same lemma gives

Poln⁡(Φn​(F))=Symn⁡F=F.\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(\Phi_{n}(F))=\operatorname{Sym}_{n}F=F.

Thus, Φn\Phi_{n} is also injective on (𝒫n,−1)Sn(\mathcal{P}_{n,-1})^{S_{n}}, and Poln\operatorname{Pol}_{n} is its inverse. ∎

Thus, describing moment invariants reduces to describing the symmetric component of 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1}. This approach is analogous to the symbolic method of classical invariant theory: moment polynomials are represented by compact multipoint moment kernels that are relative invariants of weight −1-1.

The cases n=1n=1 and n=2n=2 require separate consideration.

Theorem 4.2.

For the diagonal projective action on one or two first jets,

𝒫1,−1=0,𝒫2,−1=0.\mathcal{P}_{1,-1}=0,\qquad\mathcal{P}_{2,-1}=0.
Proof.

By the characterization of relative invariants of weight −1-1 in terms of the Lie algebra action, every polynomial F∈𝒫n,−1F\in\mathcal{P}_{n,-1} satisfies the system

ℒk[n]F=0,k=1,…,8.\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}F=0,\qquad k=1,\ldots,8.

First, consider the case n=1n=1. Let F=F⁡(x,y,p,q)∈𝒫1,−1.F=F(x,y,p,q)\in\mathcal{P}_{1,-1}. For the translation generators X1=∂x,X2=∂y,X_{1}=\partial_{x},X_{2}=\partial_{y}, we have div⁡X1=div⁡X2=0,\operatorname{div}X_{1}=\operatorname{div}X_{2}=0, and their first prolongations coincide with the generators themselves. Therefore, the corresponding operators on the space of a single first jet take the form

ℒ1[1]=∂x,ℒ2[1]=∂y.\mathscr{L}_{1}^{[1]}=\partial_{x},\qquad\mathscr{L}_{2}^{[1]}=\partial_{y}.

The conditions

ℒ1[1]​F=0,ℒ2[1]​F=0\mathscr{L}_{1}^{[1]}F=0,\qquad\mathscr{L}_{2}^{[1]}F=0

give the system

∂F∂x=0,∂F∂y=0.\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=0,\qquad\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=0.

Thus, FF does not depend on xx and yy, that is, F=F⁡(p,q).F=F(p,q).

For the generators X3=x∂x,X4=y∂y,X_{3}=x\partial_{x},X_{4}=y\partial_{y}, we have div⁡X3=1,div⁡X4=1,\operatorname{div}X_{3}=1,\operatorname{div}X_{4}=1, and their first prolongations take the form

X3(1)=x∂x−p∂p,X4(1)=y∂y−q∂q.X_{3}^{(1)}=x\partial_{x}-p\partial_{p},\qquad X_{4}^{(1)}=y\partial_{y}-q\partial_{q}.

Therefore, the corresponding operators on the space of a single first jet are

ℒ3[1]=x∂x−p∂p+1,ℒ4[1]=y∂y−q∂q+1.\mathscr{L}_{3}^{[1]}=x\partial_{x}-p\partial_{p}+1,\qquad\mathscr{L}_{4}^{[1]}=y\partial_{y}-q\partial_{q}+1.

Since we have already established that F=F⁡(p,q)F=F(p,q), the conditions

ℒ3[1]​F=0,ℒ4[1]​F=0\mathscr{L}_{3}^{[1]}F=0,\qquad\mathscr{L}_{4}^{[1]}F=0

take the form

−p​∂F∂p+F=0,−q​∂F∂q+F=0,-p\frac{\partial F}{\partial p}+F=0,\qquad-q\frac{\partial F}{\partial q}+F=0,

or, equivalently,

p​∂F∂p=F,q​∂F∂q=F.p\frac{\partial F}{\partial p}=F,\qquad q\frac{\partial F}{\partial q}=F.

The first equality means that FF is homogeneous of degree 11 in the variable pp, while the second means that it is homogeneous of degree 11 in the variable qq. Since FF is a polynomial, it follows that

F=c​p​qF=c\,pq

for some constant cc.

Now, for the generator X5=y∂x,X_{5}=y\partial_{x}, we have ℒ5[1]=y∂x−p∂q.\mathscr{L}_{5}^{[1]}=y\partial_{x}-p\partial_{q}. Hence,

0=ℒ5[1]​F=−p​∂∂q​(c​p​q)=−c​p2,0=\mathscr{L}_{5}^{[1]}F=-p\frac{\partial}{\partial q}(cpq)=-cp^{2},

so c=0c=0. Thus, 𝒫1,−1=0.\mathcal{P}_{1,-1}=0.

We now turn to the case n=2n=2. Let F=F⁡(x1,y1,p1,q1,x2,y2,p2,q2)∈𝒫2,−1.F=F(x_{1},y_{1},p_{1},q_{1},x_{2},y_{2},p_{2},q_{2})\in\mathcal{P}_{2,-1}. As in the case of a single jet, we first use the translation generators. For these,

ℒ1[2]=∂x1+∂x2,ℒ2[2]=∂y1+∂y2.\mathscr{L}_{1}^{[2]}=\partial_{x_{1}}+\partial_{x_{2}},\qquad\mathscr{L}_{2}^{[2]}=\partial_{y_{1}}+\partial_{y_{2}}.

Therefore, the equations

ℒ1[2]​F=0,ℒ2[2]​F=0\mathscr{L}_{1}^{[2]}F=0,\qquad\mathscr{L}_{2}^{[2]}F=0

mean that FF depends on the coordinates of the two points only through their differences

u=x2−x1,v=y2−y1.u=x_{2}-x_{1},\qquad v=y_{2}-y_{1}.

Thus, F=F⁡(u,v,p1,q1,p2,q2).F=F(u,v,p_{1},q_{1},p_{2},q_{2}).

We now show that FF vanishes on the hyperplane v=0v=0. For the generator X8=xy∂x+y2∂y,X_{8}=xy\partial_{x}+y^{2}\partial_{y}, we have the following first prolongation:

ℒ8=xy∂x+y2∂y−yp∂p−(xp+2yq)∂q+3y.\mathscr{L}_{8}=xy\partial_{x}+y^{2}\partial_{y}-yp\partial_{p}-(xp+2yq)\partial_{q}+3y.

4.5. Derivative degree and integral identities

The structural description of admissible monomials gives an important restriction on the moments that occur in the invariants.

Lemma 4.2.

Let 𝒟​𝒫≥3=ℝ⁡[mα,β,r,s∣r+s≥3]\mathcal{DP}_{\geq 3}=\mathbb{R}[m_{\alpha,\beta,r,s}\mid r+s\geq 3]. For every n≥3n\geq 3, we have ℳ​ℐn⊂𝒟​𝒫≥3\mathcal{MI}_{n}\subset\mathcal{DP}_{\geq 3}.

Proof.

For an admissible monomial (7), the degree in the derivatives pi,qip_{i},q_{i} equals

d𝒃​(i)+∑j≠iai​j=3+∑j≠iaj​i≥3,d_{\boldsymbol{b}}(i)+\sum_{j\neq i}a_{ij}=3+\sum_{j\neq i}a_{ji}\geq 3,

where (8) has been used. Thus, each moment factor in its image under Φn\Phi_{n} has r+s≥3r+s\geq 3. The assertion follows from the description of 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1} by admissible monomials and Theorem 4.1. ∎

On the entire algebra 𝒟​𝒫\mathcal{DP}, the integral realization (12) is not injective. For example, we have

m0,0,1,0​(f)=12​∬ℝ2∂x(f2)​𝑑x​𝑑y=0.m_{0,0,1,0}(f)=\frac{1}{2}\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\partial_{x}(f^{2})\,dx\,dy=0.

However, as the following theorem shows, there are no universal polynomial identities on the subalgebra from Lemma 4.2.

Theorem 4.3.

Let P1,…,PN∈ℝ⁡[x,y,p,q]P_{1},\ldots,P_{N}\in\mathbb{R}[x,y,p,q] be linearly independent, and suppose that each of their monomials has degree in p,qp,q at least two. Then the functionals

Mi(f)=∬ℝ2f(x,y)Pi(x,y,p,q)dxdy,i=1,…,N,M_{i}(f)=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}f(x,y)P_{i}(x,y,p,q)\,dx\,dy,\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,

are algebraically independent on the class of twice-differentiable functions ff with compact support. In particular, the integral realization of the algebra 𝒟​𝒫≥3\mathcal{DP}_{\geq 3} is injective.

Proof.

For the proof, we use standard methods of the calculus of variations for functionals depending on the function ff and its first derivatives. Let EiE_{i} denote

Ei=Pi−Dx​(f​∂Pi∂p)−Dy​(f​∂Pi∂q).E_{i}=P_{i}-D_{x}\!\left(f\frac{\partial P_{i}}{\partial p}\right)-D_{y}\!\left(f\frac{\partial P_{i}}{\partial q}\right).

the Euler–Lagrange expression for the integrand f​PifP_{i}. Then, after simplification and integration by parts, the first variation of the functional MiM_{i} takes the form

D​Mi​(f)​[h]=∫ℝ2Ei​(j2​f)​h​𝑑x​𝑑y,DM_{i}(f)[h]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}E_{i}(j^{2}f)\,h\,dx\,dy,

where j2​f=(x,y,f,p,q,fx​x,fx​y,fy​y)j^{2}f=(x,y,f,p,q,f_{xx},f_{xy},f_{yy}) is the second jet of the function ff.

We first prove that E1,…,ENE_{1},\ldots,E_{N} are linearly independent as functions on the second-jet space. Suppose that ∑ici​Ei=0\sum_{i}c_{i}E_{i}=0, and let P=∑ici​PiP=\sum_{i}c_{i}P_{i}. Then the Euler–Lagrange expression for f​PfP vanishes identically. Its coefficients of fx​x,fx​y,fy​yf_{xx},f_{xy},f_{yy} are −f​Pp​p-fP_{pp}, −2​f​Pp​q-2fP_{pq}, and −f​Pq​q-fP_{qq}, respectively. Since the equality holds for all jet values, we have Pp​p=Pp​q=Pq​q=0P_{pp}=P_{pq}=P_{qq}=0. Thus, PP has degree at most one in the variables p,qp,q. However, all monomials of PP have degree in p,qp,q at least two, so P=0P=0. The linear independence of the PiP_{i} now gives c1=⋯=cN=0c_{1}=\cdots=c_{N}=0.

Thus, the vectors of values (E1​(θ),…,EN​(θ))(E_{1}(\theta),\ldots,E_{N}(\theta)) span ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}. Choose jets θ1,…,θN\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{N} such that the matrix

A=(Ei​(θj))i,j=1NA=\bigl(E_{i}(\theta_{j})\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{N}

is nonsingular. Since the determinant of AA depends continuously on the jet coordinates and is nonzero, it remains nonzero under sufficiently small perturbations. Therefore, the base points (xj,yj)(x_{j},y_{j}) can be chosen to be pairwise distinct without affecting the nonsingularity of the matrix.

These jets can be realized by a single twice-differentiable function f∗f_{*}. Indeed, near each base point (xj,yj)(x_{j},y_{j}), choose a quadratic polynomial whose second jet at that point coincides with the prescribed jet θj\theta_{j}. Next, multiply this polynomial by a smooth function χj\chi_{j} that equals 11 in a neighborhood of (xj,yj)(x_{j},y_{j}) and equals 00 outside a slightly larger neighborhood. Multiplication by χj\chi_{j} therefore does not change the value of the polynomial or its derivatives up to second order at (xj,yj)(x_{j},y_{j}). Since the base points are pairwise distinct, these neighborhoods can be chosen to be pairwise disjoint. The sum of the resulting localized polynomials gives a compactly supported function f∗f_{*} such that

j2f∗(xj,yj)=θj,j=1,…,N.j^{2}f_{*}(x_{j},y_{j})=\theta_{j},\qquad j=1,\ldots,N.

Now choose nonnegative twice-differentiable functions hjh_{j} with unit integral and supports in small neighborhoods of the corresponding points. By the continuity of Ei​(j2​f∗)E_{i}(j^{2}f_{*}), as these supports shrink, we have

D​Mi​(f∗)​[hj]=∫ℝ2Ei​(j2​f∗)​hj​𝑑x​𝑑y⟶Ei​(θj).DM_{i}(f_{*})[h_{j}]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}E_{i}(j^{2}f_{*})h_{j}\,dx\,dy\longrightarrow E_{i}(\theta_{j}).

Thus, the supports can be chosen so that the matrix B=(D​Mi​(f∗)​[hj])i,j=1NB=(DM_{i}(f_{*})[h_{j}])_{i,j=1}^{N} is nonsingular.

Consider the map

Ψ:ℝN⟶ℝN,Ψ⁡(t)=(Mi​(f∗+∑j=1Ntj​hj))i=1N.\Psi:\mathbb{R}^{N}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{N},\qquad\Psi(t)=\left(M_{i}\left(f_{*}+\sum_{j=1}^{N}t_{j}h_{j}\right)\right)_{i=1}^{N}.

It is polynomial in tt, and its Jacobian matrix at zero equals BB. By the inverse function theorem, the image of Ψ\Psi contains an open subset of ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}.

If there were a polynomial RR such that R⁡(M1​(f),…,MN​(f))=0R(M_{1}(f),\ldots,M_{N}(f))=0 for all admissible ff, it would vanish on this open subset. Therefore, RR would be the zero polynomial, proving the algebraic independence of the functionals.

Finally, every polynomial in 𝒟​𝒫≥3\mathcal{DP}_{\geq 3} depends on only finitely many moment generators. Their distinct monomial kernels xα​yβ​pr​qsx^{\alpha}y^{\beta}p^{r}q^{s}, r+s≥3r+s\geq 3, satisfy the hypotheses of the assertion just proved. Thus, no nonzero element of 𝒟​𝒫≥3\mathcal{DP}_{\geq 3} is realized as the zero functional, that is, the integral realization of this algebra is injective. ∎

Thus, the passage from formal moment variables to their integral definitions does not produce additional algebraic relations among the constructed invariants.

5. Low-Order Projective Differential Moment Invariants

Theorem 4.1 reduces the construction of moment invariants to the description of symmetric relative invariants of weight −1-1. In this section, we consider explicit constructions of moment degrees 33 and 44.

5.1. Moment invariants of degrees 11 and 22

Before turning to the first nontrivial constructions of moment degree 33, we consider the two lower degrees. Theorem 4.2 shows that the corresponding spaces of relative invariants of weight −1-1 for one and two first jets are zero, which immediately leads to the following assertion.

Theorem 5.1.

There are no nonzero projective differential moment invariants of moment degrees 11 and 22:

ℳ​ℐ1=ℳ​ℐ2={0}.\mathcal{MI}_{1}=\mathcal{MI}_{2}=\{0\}.

Let I∈ℳ​ℐnI\in\mathcal{MI}_{n}, where n=1n=1 or n=2n=2. By the property of polarization that intertwines the corresponding Lie algebra actions,

Poln(𝒟kI)=ℒk[n]Poln(I),k=1,…,8.\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(\mathscr{D}_{k}I)=\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(I),\qquad k=1,\ldots,8.

ℒk[n]Poln(I)=0,k=1,…,8.\mathscr{L}_{k}^{[n]}\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(I)=0,\qquad k=1,\ldots,8.

Thus, Poln⁡(I)∈𝒫n,−1.\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(I)\in\mathcal{P}_{n,-1}. By Theorem 4.2, 𝒫1,−1=𝒫2,−1=0,\mathcal{P}_{1,-1}=\mathcal{P}_{2,-1}=0, so Poln⁡(I)=0.\operatorname{Pol}_{n}(I)=0. Therefore, there are no nonzero moment invariants of degrees 11 and 22. ∎

μi​j​k=(−1)k​ϕ00​i​j​k.\mu_{ijk}=(-1)^{k}\phi_{00ijk}.

Thus, both systems of moments span the same space W0W_{0}.

5.3. Moment degree three

We first prove Theorem 2.2, which gives a general description of invariants of moment degree 33.

Proof of Theorem 2.2.

By the theorem on the structure of the space 𝒫n,−1\mathcal{P}_{n,-1}, each of its elements is a linear combination of admissible monomials P𝒃,𝒂.P_{\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{a}}. For n=3n=3, the set 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} contains only the triple {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\}. Therefore, the first admissibility condition ∑I∈𝒯3bI=3\sum_{I\in\mathcal{T}_{3}}b_{I}=3 gives b123=3.b_{123}=3. so the second admissibility condition takes the form ∂𝒂(i)=0,i=1,2,3.\partial_{\boldsymbol{a}}(i)=0,\qquad i=1,2,3. This means that, for each index, the total number of its occurrences as the first index in the factors Ci​jC_{ij} equals the total number of its occurrences as the second index. Therefore, the corresponding monomial in Ci​jC_{ij} decomposes into a product of closed cycles. For three indices, these cycles are 𝖷,𝖸,𝖹,U,V;\mathsf{X},\mathsf{Y},\mathsf{Z},U,V; see (2) and (3). for some polynomial QQ.

Therefore, the product (18) is symmetric under permutations of the points if and only if QQ changes sign under every odd permutation, that is, if it is antisymmetric.

By Theorem 4.1, the map Φ3\Phi_{3} establishes a one-to-one correspondence between symmetric elements of 𝒫3,−1\mathcal{P}_{3,-1} and moment invariants in ℳ​ℐ3\mathcal{MI}_{3}. Therefore, every I∈ℳ​ℐ3I\in\mathcal{MI}_{3} has the form

I=Φ3​(D123 3​Q​(𝖷,𝖸,𝖹,U,V)),I=\Phi_{3}\left(D_{123}^{\,3}Q(\mathsf{X},\mathsf{Y},\mathsf{Z},U,V)\right),

where QQ is antisymmetric, and every such expression is a moment invariant. ∎

The constructed family of invariants Ja,kJ_{a,k} allows us to establish an important structural property of the algebra of moment invariants: it has no finite generating system.

Theorem 5.2.

The space ℳ​ℐ3\mathcal{MI}_{3} is infinite-dimensional. The algebra ℳ​ℐ\mathcal{MI} is not finitely generated as an ℝ\mathbb{R}-algebra.

Proof.

Assign to the moment generator mα,β,r,sm_{\alpha,\beta,r,s} the auxiliary degree r+sr+s, and extend it to moment monomials by adding the degrees of their factors.

By Theorem 2.3, for every a≥1a\geq 1, the invariant Ja,0J_{a,0} is nonzero and belongs to ℳ​ℐ3\mathcal{MI}_{3}. Each of its moment factors has derivative degree a+3a+3, so Ja,0J_{a,0} is homogeneous of auxiliary degree 3​(a+3)3(a+3). These degrees are pairwise distinct, so the invariants Ja,0J_{a,0}, a≥1a\geq 1, are linearly independent. Thus,

dimℝℳ​ℐ3=∞.\dim_{\mathbb{R}}\mathcal{MI}_{3}=\infty.

Suppose that ℳ​ℐ\mathcal{MI} is finitely generated. Since the operators 𝒟k\mathscr{D}_{k} preserve moment degree, each homogeneous component of a moment invariant is also an invariant. Replacing a finite generating system with the homogeneous components of its generators gives a finite system of homogeneous generators.

However, ℳ​ℐ0=ℝ\mathcal{MI}_{0}=\mathbb{R} and ℳ​ℐ1=ℳ​ℐ2=0\mathcal{MI}_{1}=\mathcal{MI}_{2}=0. Therefore, all nonzero generators of positive degree have moment degree at least 33. Products of two or more such factors have degree at least 66. Thus, ℳ​ℐ3\mathcal{MI}_{3} would have to be the linear span of finitely many generators of degree 33, contradicting its infinite dimensionality. ∎

We next consider several explicit examples of the simplest invariants of degree 33 :

I5(3)\displaystyle I^{(3)}_{5} =Φ3​(D123 3​(U−V))=J1,0,\displaystyle=\Phi_{3}\left(D_{123}^{\,3}(U-V)\right)=J_{1,0},

I7,2(3)\displaystyle I^{(3)}_{7,2} =Φ3​(D123 3​(U2−V2)).\displaystyle=\Phi_{3}\left(D_{123}^{\,3}(U^{2}-V^{2})\right).

Table 1 gives the number of monomials after expanding the kernels and collecting like terms, as well as the number of distinct DD-moments used. No additional linear relations between DD-moments are applied in this process. Thus, the reported numbers characterize these particular representations rather than the minimum possible complexity of the invariants.

5.4. Moment degree four

For moment degree 44, the basic construction is the kernel

(19) P0=D123​D124​D134​D234.P_{0}=D_{123}D_{124}D_{134}D_{234}.

Each index occurs in exactly three determinants, so, by the conditions (8), P0P_{0} has relative weight −1-1. Moreover, each adjacent transposition changes the signs of two determinants and interchanges the others. Thus, P0P_{0} is symmetric in the point labels.

The corresponding moment invariant takes the form

I3(4)=Φ4​(P0)=24​S,I^{(4)}_{3}=\Phi_{4}(P_{0})=24S,

where SS is normalized according to the polynomial (1). Its displayed DD-moment representation has order 33 and contains 2525 monomials in 1010 distinct moments.

The determinant representations of the invariants SS and TT are given in Subsection 2.2. Both use moments from W0W_{0}, but have different moment degrees: 44 for SS and 66 for TT.

New examples of invariants of DD-order 55 can be obtained by multiplying P0P_{0} by symmetric polynomials in Ci​jC_{ij} that are unchanged under projective transformations. Consider

E2\displaystyle E_{2} =∑1≤i<j≤4Ci​j​Cj​i,\displaystyle=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq 4}C_{ij}C_{ji},
E3\displaystyle E_{3} =∑1≤i<j<k≤4(Ci​j​Cj​k​Ck​i+Ci​k​Ck​j​Cj​i),\displaystyle=\sum_{1\leq i<j<k\leq 4}\left(C_{ij}C_{jk}C_{ki}+C_{ik}C_{kj}C_{ji}\right),
E4\displaystyle E_{4} =∑(i,j,k)∈Perm⁡(2,3,4)C1​i​Ci​j​Cj​k​Ck​1,\displaystyle=\sum_{(i,j,k)\in\operatorname{Perm}(2,3,4)}C_{1i}C_{ij}C_{jk}C_{k1},

where Perm⁡(2,3,4)\operatorname{Perm}(2,3,4) denotes the six permutations of the triple (2,3,4)(2,3,4).

All of E2,E3,E4E_{2},E_{3},E_{4} are symmetric absolute invariants. Accordingly, the kernels P0​E2P_{0}E_{2}, P0​E3P_{0}E_{3}, and P0​E4P_{0}E_{4} remain symmetric and retain relative weight −1-1.

We obtain three moment invariants

I5,1(4)=Φ4​(P0​E2),I5,2(4)=Φ4​(P0​E3),I5,3(4)=Φ4​(P0​E4).I^{(4)}_{5,1}=\Phi_{4}(P_{0}E_{2}),\quad I^{(4)}_{5,2}=\Phi_{4}(P_{0}E_{3}),\quad I^{(4)}_{5,3}=\Phi_{4}(P_{0}E_{4}).

These numbers show that, even at a fixed moment degree, increasing the DD-order substantially increases the complexity of the moment expansion.

5.5. What about rational differential moment invariants?

The action of the Lie algebra 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3} on the moment algebra 𝒟​𝒫\mathcal{DP} naturally extends to its field of fractions 𝒦=Frac⁡(𝒟​𝒫),\mathcal{K}=\operatorname{Frac}(\mathcal{DP}), and let 𝒦𝔰​𝔩3\mathcal{K}^{\mathfrak{sl}_{3}} denote the field of 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3}-invariants. It turns out that, in this case, rational invariants do not form a fundamentally broader class than polynomial invariants.

Theorem 5.3.

The following equality holds:

𝒦𝔰​𝔩3=Frac⁡(ℳ​ℐ).\mathcal{K}^{\mathfrak{sl}_{3}}=\operatorname{Frac}(\mathcal{MI}).

Thus, every rational projective differential moment invariant can be expressed as a ratio of two polynomial moment invariants.

This assertion is analogous to the standard result of classical invariant theory concerning the field of rational invariants of a factorial algebra under the action of a semisimple algebraic group [15, 16]. Since, in our case, 𝒟​𝒫\mathcal{DP} has an infinite set of generators and invariance is defined directly through the action of the Lie algebra 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3}, we give a short direct proof.

Proof.

Let

R=PQ∈𝒦𝔰​𝔩3,P,Q∈𝒟​𝒫,gcd⁡(P,Q)=1.R=\frac{P}{Q}\in\mathcal{K}^{\mathfrak{sl}_{3}},\qquad P,Q\in\mathcal{DP},\qquad\gcd(P,Q)=1.

For every X∈𝔰​𝔩3X\in\mathfrak{sl}_{3}, we have 𝒟X​R=0,\mathscr{D}_{X}R=0, and hence Q​𝒟X​P−P​𝒟X​Q=0.Q\,\mathscr{D}_{X}P-P\,\mathscr{D}_{X}Q=0. Since PP and QQ are relatively prime, this equality implies

P∣𝒟XP,Q∣𝒟XQ.P\mid\mathscr{D}_{X}P,\qquad Q\mid\mathscr{D}_{X}Q.

Thus, for some hX∈𝒟​𝒫h_{X}\in\mathcal{DP}, we have

𝒟X​P=hX​P,𝒟X​Q=hX​Q.\mathscr{D}_{X}P=h_{X}P,\qquad\mathscr{D}_{X}Q=h_{X}Q.

Here, we may assume that P,Q≠0P,Q\neq 0, since the case R=0R=0 is immediate. Let degm\deg_{m} denote the maximum total degree of a polynomial in the moment variables. The operator 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X} preserves each homogeneous component, so degm⁡(𝒟X​P)≤degm⁡P\deg_{m}(\mathscr{D}_{X}P)\leq\deg_{m}P. If hX≠0h_{X}\neq 0, then

degm⁡(hX​P)=degm⁡hX+degm⁡P,\deg_{m}(h_{X}P)=\deg_{m}h_{X}+\deg_{m}P,

and hence degm⁡hX=0\deg_{m}h_{X}=0. Thus, hX=λX∈ℝh_{X}=\lambda_{X}\in\mathbb{R}; homogeneity of PP and QQ is not required.

The map X↦λXX\mapsto\lambda_{X} is linear. Under the standard convention for the commutator of vector fields, we have

[X(1),Y(1)]=[X,Y](1),div⁡[X,Y]=X⁡(div⁡Y)−Y⁡(div⁡X).[X^{(1)},Y^{(1)}]=[X,Y]^{(1)},\qquad\operatorname{div}[X,Y]=X(\operatorname{div}Y)-Y(\operatorname{div}X).

Therefore, the weighted operators ℒX=X(1)+div⁡X\mathscr{L}_{X}=X^{(1)}+\operatorname{div}X satisfy [ℒX,ℒY]=ℒ[X,Y][\mathscr{L}_{X},\mathscr{L}_{Y}]=\mathscr{L}_{[X,Y]}. By the definition of the action on moment generators, this gives [𝒟X,𝒟Y]=𝒟[X,Y].[\mathscr{D}_{X},\mathscr{D}_{Y}]=\mathscr{D}_{[X,Y]}. Applying this identity to PP, we obtain

λ[X,Y]​P=[𝒟X,𝒟Y]​P=(λY​λX−λX​λY)​P=0.\lambda_{[X,Y]}P=[\mathscr{D}_{X},\mathscr{D}_{Y}]P=(\lambda_{Y}\lambda_{X}-\lambda_{X}\lambda_{Y})P=0.

Since P≠0P\neq 0, we have λ[X,Y]=0\lambda_{[X,Y]}=0. Since 𝔰​𝔩3=[𝔰​𝔩3,𝔰​𝔩3],\mathfrak{sl}_{3}=[\mathfrak{sl}_{3},\mathfrak{sl}_{3}], and the character λ\lambda vanishes on all commutators, λ⁡([X,Y])=0\lambda([X,Y])=0, it vanishes identically on the entire algebra 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3}. Hence, λX=0\lambda_{X}=0 for all X∈𝔰​𝔩3.X\in\mathfrak{sl}_{3}. Thus, 𝒟X​P=𝒟X​Q=0,\mathscr{D}_{X}P=\mathscr{D}_{X}Q=0, that is, P,Q∈ℳ​ℐP,Q\in\mathcal{MI}. Therefore,

R=PQ∈Frac⁡(ℳ​ℐ).R=\frac{P}{Q}\in\operatorname{Frac}(\mathcal{MI}).

The reverse inclusion is immediate. ∎

Thus, under the definition of projective invariance adopted in this paper through the Lie algebra action, passing to rational functions produces no new invariants: the field of rational invariants is the field of fractions of the algebra of polynomial invariants.

This situation differs fundamentally from the case of the full affine group, which has nontrivial characters. Therefore, for affine moments, there may exist rational invariants whose numerator and denominator are not individually polynomial absolute invariants. This is precisely the mechanism underlying the classical rational affine moment invariants of Flusser–Suk [17]. For the action of 𝔰​𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_{3}, this mechanism is impossible, since 𝔰​𝔩3=[𝔰​𝔩3,𝔰​𝔩3],\mathfrak{sl}_{3}=[\mathfrak{sl}_{3},\mathfrak{sl}_{3}], and hence this Lie algebra has no nontrivial characters.

Code availability

The implementation is available at

https://github.com/LeonidBed/projective-differential-moment-invariants.

The repository provides routines for computing SS, TT, and the degree-three invariants denoted in the code by I3_cycle, I3_cycle_edge, and I3_cycle_square. The implementation supports the computational use of the moment constructions developed in this paper.

6. Conclusion

This paper develops an algebraic framework for describing polynomial first-order projective differential moment invariants. The main result is a one-to-one correspondence established for every n≥1n\geq 1,

Φn:(𝒫n,−1)Sn⟶ℳ​ℐn,Φn−1=Poln,\Phi_{n}:(\mathcal{P}_{n,-1})^{S_{n}}\longrightarrow\mathcal{MI}_{n},\qquad\Phi_{n}^{-1}=\operatorname{Pol}_{n},

between moment invariants of degree nn and symmetric nn-point polynomial relative projective invariants of weight −1-1. Thus, the problem of constructing moment invariants reduces to the already described algebraic problem of constructing multipoint relative invariants. The injectivity of the integral realization on the subalgebra of moments arising in these constructions ensures that the formal algebraic results carry over to the corresponding image functionals.

Explicit results are obtained for low moment degrees. The absence of nonzero invariants of degrees 11 and 22 is proved, and a complete description of invariants of degree 33 is obtained through symmetrized multipoint kernels. The ten cubic differential moments form a module equivalent to the space of ternary cubics, so the classical Aronhold invariants SS and TT generate projective differential moment invariants of degrees 44 and 66. In particular, this connection explains the invariant-theoretic nature of the known 25-term expression Inv2,0\operatorname{Inv}_{2,0} [5].

The infinite dimensionality of the space ℳ​ℐ3\mathcal{MI}_{3} and the absence of a finite generating system for the algebra ℳ​ℐ\mathcal{MI} are also established. At the same time, every rational moment invariant is a ratio of two polynomial moment invariants. Thus, the field of rational moment invariants is completely determined by the algebra ℳ​ℐ\mathcal{MI}.

Compact multipoint representations provide a constructive passage from relative invariants to moment polynomials and serve as a basis for their software computation. This connects the algebraic results obtained with the construction of invariant image characteristics for image analysis and pattern recognition tasks.

Further development of this approach involves designing numerically stable methods for computing the constructed invariants on digital images, using orthogonal moments, and evaluating the discriminative power of the resulting characteristics in image analysis and pattern recognition tasks.
